title: Skill set: Boundaries
description: Ten questions on joining and separating clauses: semicolons, colons, dashes, commas, and when to use no punctuation at all.

questions.passage: The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the ______ by the 2000s, much of its former bed had become desert.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
Both parts are complete sentences: *The Aral Sea was once the fourth-largest lake in the world* and *by the 2000s, much of its former bed had become desert*. A semicolon can join two complete sentences, so **world;** is right.

A comma alone (A) joins two sentences with only a comma, a comma splice. No punctuation (B) runs them together. D adds *which*, but *which by the 2000s, much of its former bed had become desert* is not a clause that works: *which* has no role in it.

questions.passage: The architects who designed the city's new ______ large windows along the north wall so that readers would have steady, indirect light.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
The subject is *the architects who designed the city's new library*, and its verb is *placed*. Nothing should separate a subject from its verb, so **library placed** is right.

A comma (A) and a dash (D) both cut the subject off from its verb. A semicolon (C) must have a complete sentence on each side, and *The architects who designed the city's new library* is not one.

questions.passage: Visitors to the museum's textile hall can see three kinds of traditional Uzbek ______ ikat-dyed silk, hand-embroidered suzanis, and cotton woven on narrow looms.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
The first part is a complete sentence that announces "three kinds," and the list that follows names them. A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence, so **textiles:** is right.

A semicolon (A) needs a complete sentence after it, and a list is not one. With no punctuation (B), the list runs straight into the sentence. *Which* (C) starts a clause that never gets a verb.

questions.passage: Nodira, a nineteenth-century poet who wrote in both Uzbek and ______ is also remembered for her role in the politics of the Kokand Khanate.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
*A nineteenth-century poet who wrote in both Uzbek and Persian* is extra information about Nodira. It opens with a comma after *Nodira*, so it must close with a comma: **Persian,**. Then the sentence continues: *Nodira ... is also remembered*.

A dash (B) cannot close a phrase that a comma opened; the pair must match. A semicolon (C) separates the subject *Nodira* from its verb *is*. With no punctuation (D), the extra phrase is never closed, and the sentence reads as if *Persian* is what "is also remembered."

questions.passage: The regional science fair drew students from Samarkand, Uzbekistan; Almaty, Kazakhstan ______ and Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
Each item in this list already contains a comma (city, country). When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items, and the first item already ends with one. So the second item must end the same way: **Kazakhstan;**.

A comma (A) makes it unclear where one item ends and the next begins. A colon (B) introduces something after a complete sentence; it does not separate list items. No punctuation (C) runs the last two items together.

questions.passage: The ______ a hardy plant that can survive on very little rain—helps keep loose desert sand from blowing away.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
*A hardy plant that can survive on very little rain* is extra information about the saxaul. It closes with a dash before *helps*, so it must open with a dash: **saxaul—**.

A comma (B) opens with one kind of punctuation and closes with another; the pair must match. A semicolon (C) needs a complete sentence before it, and *The saxaul* is not one. With no punctuation (D), the sentence reads *The saxaul a hardy plant*, and the closing dash has nothing to pair with.

questions.passage: During a long-term field project, marine ______ recorded thousands of the clicking sounds that sperm whales use to communicate.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
*Marine biologist* works as a title in front of the name, like *Doctor* or *Professor*, and the name tells us which biologist. A title directly before a name takes no punctuation, and the subject *marine biologist Ana Ferreira* should not be separated from the verb *recorded*. So **biologist Ana Ferreira** is right.

A puts commas around the name as if it could be removed, but without it the sentence reads *marine biologist recorded*, which is missing a word like *a*. B puts a comma between the subject and its verb. D separates the title from the name with a single comma that is never closed.

questions.passage: The first trial of the new wheat variety produced disappointing ______ the second trial, conducted after farmers adjusted the irrigation schedule, yielded nearly twice as much grain.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
There are two complete sentences here, and *however* is a transition word, not a conjunction like *but*. It cannot join two sentences with commas alone. The standard pattern is a semicolon before *however* and a comma after it: **results; however,**.

A joins the two sentences with only commas, a comma splice. C has the same problem and also drops the comma after *however*. D has no punctuation at all between the two sentences.

questions.passage: Ornithologists tracking white storks wanted to know whether the birds followed the same migration route every ______ To find out, they fitted twenty storks with lightweight GPS tags.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
The first sentence is a statement that *reports* a question (*wanted to know whether ...*). It does not ask one, so it ends with a period: **year.** The capital *T* in *To find out* also shows that a new sentence begins.

A question mark (B) is only for a direct question, such as *Do the birds follow the same route?* A comma (C) joins two complete sentences with only a comma, a comma splice. No punctuation (D) runs them together.

questions.passage: Many reptiles of the Kyzylkum ______ the desert monitor and the toad-headed agama, escape the midday heat by sheltering in burrows.
questions.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.explanation:
*Such as the desert monitor and the toad-headed agama* is a group of examples that could be removed. It already closes with a comma after *agama*, so it must open with a comma: **Desert, such as**. Remove it and the sentence still works: *Many reptiles of the Kyzylkum Desert escape the midday heat*.

Without the opening comma (A), the comma after *agama* stands alone and separates the subject from the verb *escape*. A colon (B) and a semicolon (D) both need a complete sentence before them, and *Many reptiles of the Kyzylkum Desert* is not one.
